Below, the season’s mean deceit—that everything stays white and clean. It doesn’t, of course, but I wish it. My prayersare green with this intent, imploring winter wrens to trill and begging scuttling bucks come back. Let larksong shudder to its January wheeze,but gift these hands a happinessjust once. It is half passed. And I am cold. Another peal has tolled.I’ve told the sum of my appeals.I need not watch for fox. They do not congregate at dawn.But I would, were I one.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, Distant, And

outputs.L1:
5 a.m. One quarter past.  
Distant chimes inform me of this.  
A peal of bells knells through the mist,  
and sunlight is not yet bludgeoning.  
But some light gets the blood going.

Last night, it was snowing,  
and now every path is a pall,  
though mine are the only footfalls  
at this hour of awe.

Above hangs a canopy of needle-leaf.  
Below lies the season’s mean deceit:  
that everything stays white and clean.  
It doesn’t, of course, but I wish it did.

My prayers are green with this intent,  
imploring winter wrens to trill  
and begging scuttling bucks to come back.  
There is something that I lack.

A wryneck bullet-beaks a branch.  
His woodworm didn’t stand a chance.

What I miss, I’ve never had.  
But I am not a ghost.  
I am a guest.  
And life is thirst, at best.

So do not strike me, Heart.  
I, too, am tinder.  
I’m as flammable as birch bark,  
even damp.

Blue spruce, bee-eater—  
be sweeter to me.  
Let larksong shudder  
to its January wheeze,  
but gift these hands a happiness  
just once.

It is half past,  
and I am cold.  
Another peal has tolled.  
I’ve told the sum of my appeals.

I need not watch for foxes.  
They do not congregate at dawn.  
But I would, were I one.
outputs.L2:
It is 5:15 a.m.; far-off bells announce the time. Their ringing sounds through the fog, while the sun has not yet begun its assault. Still, the faintest brightness stirs my blood.

Snow fell overnight, and every trail now wears a shroud. At this solemn hour, my footprints are the only ones. Overhead, conifer needles form a roof; underfoot lies the season’s cruel illusion that all things can remain spotless and white. They cannot, though I want them to.

That longing colors my prayers green. I plead for winter wrens to sing and for the darting bucks to return, because something is absent from me. A wryneck drives its sharp beak into a limb; the woodworm it finds is doomed.

I yearn for something I have never possessed. Yet I am no spirit—only a visitor. Life, in its finest form, is a kind of craving. So, Heart, do not hit me. I, too, can catch fire, as easily as wet birch bark.

Blue spruce and bee-eater, show me more kindness. Let the skylark’s song tremble into its breathless January rasp, but allow these hands to hold happiness once—just once.

The quarter-hour is gone, and I am freezing. The bells have sounded again. I have now voiced every plea I carry. There is no reason to wait for a fox; foxes do not assemble at daybreak. But if I were one, I would.
outputs.L3:
At 5:15 in the morning, before sunrise, the speaker walks alone through a winter landscape veiled in snow and mist. The untouched snow makes the world appear pure, still, and permanent, yet the speaker understands that this perfection is only temporary. Beneath the beauty of the scene lies an awareness that the snow will melt and the illusion of permanence will disappear.

Surrounded by cold and silence, the speaker longs for the return of birds, deer, and other signs of life. Their absence seems to reflect a deeper, unnamed emptiness within the speaker—an emotional deprivation that the natural world cannot yet relieve. Despite feeling exposed and vulnerable, the speaker refuses to become ghostlike or detached from life. Instead, they insist on remaining a living guest in the world, present and capable of desire.

As distant bells mark the passing of time, the speaker’s longing becomes a quiet plea. In the midst of solitude, cold, and uncertainty, they ask not for lasting joy, but for a single moment of happiness: one brief experience of warmth and fullness before the frozen stillness changes.
outputs.L4:
At dawn, I walk alone across the snow-covered fields. The world is pale and silent, its roads erased beneath the night’s snowfall. Frost hangs from the branches, and the first light spreads slowly across the horizon, touching the distant hills without warming them. My footsteps are the only sound, and even they seem too small to disturb the vast winter stillness.

Birds hidden among the bare trees, have you known such loneliness? You who call to one another through the cold, lend me a song to carry on my way. Deer moving quietly at the edge of the forest, tell me where you find the courage to cross these empty fields. Even the wind appears to seek companionship as it wanders through the reeds and presses against my coat.

And you, restless heart, why do you continue to desire what the world withholds? Life has been a long thirst, a cup repeatedly lifted to the lips and found empty. I have followed distant lights, believed in voices that vanished, and waited at doors that never opened. Still, some stubborn tenderness remains within me.

For when the sun rises above the trees and the snow begins to shine, I cannot entirely surrender hope. A bird’s sudden flight, a track beside my own, or a faint curl of smoke from a faraway house is enough to awaken the old longing. Perhaps somewhere there is warmth, a welcome, and a hand reaching toward mine.

So I continue through the winter morning—alone, but not beyond hope. The cold surrounds me, yet beneath it the earth keeps its hidden seeds. My heart, though weary and unsatisfied, still turns toward the possibility of spring, connection, and happiness.
outputs.L5:
**One, Distant, And**

One light remained in the window, small against the evening sky. From the distant hills came the sound of thunder, soft and uncertain, like a memory returning. And between the light and the storm stood a traveler, wondering whether home was the place behind him—or the hope still waiting ahead.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a solitary pre-dawn walk through a snowy forest, beginning at 5:15 a.m. and ending with the speaker imagining being a fox.
counterfactuals.output:
At 5:15 a.m., the world is still folded inside its dark blue wing. I step into the snowy forest alone, my breath a small lantern that brightens nothing, then vanishes. The path has forgotten every foot that ever trusted it. Snow fills the hollows, softens the fallen branches, lays its white listening over stone and root. Above me, the pines hold their silence like water held in a cup.

I walk until the last house-light disappears behind the trees. Each step gives a brief, dry sigh. Somewhere beneath the snow, a creek continues its black dreaming. Somewhere an owl closes its eyes. The cold enters carefully—through my gloves, beneath my collar—as if searching for the warm animal I have hidden inside my name.

Then, slowly, the eastern sky loosens. Blue becomes pearl; pearl gathers a thin seam of rose. The trunks emerge one by one, dark pillars in a ruined temple, and the snow begins to shine without yet belonging to morning. I stop where the trail crosses a scatter of tracks: delicate commas, a sentence written toward the thicket and left unfinished.

For a moment, I envy whatever passed here unseen—its quick blood, its bright hunger, its freedom from clocks. I imagine slipping beneath the low branches, rust-red against the white, my ears tuned to the roots of the world, my paws touching the snow so lightly that dawn itself would not hear me. I imagine being a fox.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental winter poem rich in bird imagery, internal rhyme, wordplay, and existential longing. Include distant church bells, fresh snow, animal tracks, and the repeated awareness of passing time.
counterfactuals.output:
**White Hours**

Fresh snow—  
the field forgets its name  
and names itself again:  
blank / blanched / beginning.

A crow rows west  
through the slow overflow of sky,  
each black wing a hinge  
on which the cold swings open.

Far off, church bells—  
bronze birds beating  
their hollow wings:

*Time passes. Time passes.*

Under the pines, fox tracks stitch  
a red thought through the white,  
though no fox—only the after  
of muscle, muzzle, hunger.

Hare-print, deer-print,  
small runes pressed  
into the page’s frozen rage.  
Who wrote *I was here*  
and who erased the writer?

Chickadees chip at silence:  
quick wit, wick-lit syllables.  
A nuthatch walks headfirst  
down the world, as if gravity  
were merely another story  
we agreed to fall for.

Again the bells, diminished  
by distance, by snow:

*Time passes. Time passes.*

I stand where the creek  
keeps speaking beneath its glass—  
a dark verb, conjugating  
*go, gone, going*—  
and ask what part of me  
is water, what part winter,  
what part the listening  
that longs to outlast sound.

Above, wild geese unfasten  
the gray seam of heaven.  
Their cries: rusty keys  
to rooms with no doors.

Snow sifts. The dusk bruises blue.  
An owl opens its round question  
and will not close it.

*Who?* it asks.  
*Who?*

I answer with my breath,  
brief thief of warmth,  
a cloud already leaving.

Behind me, my tracks fill slowly.  
Before me, no tracks at all.

The bells become less bell  
than memory of bell,  
less memory than trembling air:

*Time passes. Time passes.*

And every bird is a small departure.  
And every feather falls upward  
in the mind.

Night nests in the bare trees.  
Stars start—far sparks, frost marks—  
and I, animal among animals,  
press one more footprint  
into the immaculate hour,

wanting the snow to remember,  
wanting the snow to forgive,

while under everything  
the hidden creek keeps going,

and over everything  
the dark keeps winging,

and through everything—

*Time passes.*  
*Time passes.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a melancholy, stream-of-consciousness monologue from someone walking alone at dawn in January. Make the speaker cold, emotionally vulnerable, and hungry for a happiness they have never known.
counterfactuals.output:
January dawn, and the sky is the color of a bruise pressed under glass.

I keep walking because stopping would mean admitting there is nowhere I need to be. My hands ache inside my pockets. I curl them into fists, then uncurl them, as if they might be holding something I’ve forgotten—keys, a letter, the small warm proof of another person’s hand. But there is nothing. Only lint. A receipt gone soft at the folds. My own fingers, startled by each other.

The houses are still asleep. Their windows shine faintly, yellow squares with curtains drawn, and I imagine kitchens behind them: kettles beginning to murmur, someone barefoot on the floorboards, someone saying good morning and meaning *I’m glad you’re here*. It seems impossible that such words are spoken every day. Impossible, and ordinary. That is the worst of it.

My breath leaves me in little ghosts.

I’m hungry, though not for breakfast. Or not only for breakfast. I want the thing people must feel when they turn toward home without fear. I want to know what it is to expect kindness and be right. To laugh before remembering to be careful. To wake and find happiness beside me, rumpled and warm, annoyed that I’ve stolen the blanket.

Have I ever been happy? There were moments, perhaps. Sun on a wall. Music through an open window. A peach eaten over the sink, juice running down my wrist. But those were visitors. They did not know my name. They never stayed long enough to take off their coats.

The cold finds the gap at my collar.

Morning is coming, slowly, without mercy. The trees stand black and bare against the paling sky, every branch exposed. I envy them. They have nothing left to hide and still the light comes for them.

So I walk toward it, though I don’t know why. Maybe hunger is a kind of hope. Maybe wanting is the last warm thing in me.

Maybe somewhere ahead, the day is keeping something I have never known how to ask for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense prose poem in which a forest guest addresses their own heart and begs nature—wrens, bucks, a wryneck, spruce, bee-eaters, and larks—to offer comfort. Use fragmented sentences and slant rhymes.
counterfactuals.output: Heart, hush now. Guest-heart under the green eaves, leaf-lost, grief-loosed. Wrens, stitch your small brown psalm through the bramble; mend what you cannot name. Bucks at the fern’s dim altar, lend me your antlered stillness, your dusk-trust, your musk. Wryneck, crooked oracle, turn your throat toward sorrow and worry it into song—wrong, wrung. Spruce, dark nurse, lower your resinous hands; let each needle teach me: remain, refrain. Bee-eaters, bright thieves, take the venom with the gold, the sting with the wing, and leave one blue feather for morning. Larks, little ladders of sound, climb where I cannot; carry this ache past air, past prayer. O forest, host me. O heart, unclose. Not healed. Held. Not whole—but wood-warm, wren-worn, near home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a surreal pastoral poem set at quarter past five after a night of snow. Contrast the apparent purity of the white landscape with its hidden deceit, weave in bells and woodland creatures, and close on the idea that foxes do not gather at dawn, though the narrator would if they were one.
counterfactuals.output:
At quarter past five, after the night of snow,  
the fields lie dressed as innocent kings,  
each thorn absolved, each ditch made holy,  
the black pond wearing a white glass eye.

But under the linen the mole keeps accounts,  
roots forge signatures in the dark,  
and the drifts, with their soft, untroubled faces,  
conceal every footprint they have swallowed.

From the steeple, bells fall into the orchard—  
bronze pears no branch can hold.  
A hare listens upright among cabbages;  
an owl folds the moon into its wing.

Soon deer will enter the pale arithmetic,  
adding their delicate, vanishing marks.  
The crows, in undertakers’ coats, will swear  
the world has never sinned, and mean the opposite.

Snow makes a chapel of every ruin,  
but beneath its altar the red teeth wait.  
Morning opens, blue and cold as a lie.

Foxes do not gather at dawn.  
But if I were a fox, I would.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
